definition.text: The branch of soil science that studies soil conditions as they bear on growing food and fibre.

facts.text: It is part of agronomy and so is also called soil agronomy; some regions know it as agrology.
Before pedology arose in the 19th century, agricultural soil science, or edaphology, was the only branch of soil science.
It studies the chemical, physical, biological and mineralogical makeup of soils as they relate to farming, and develops methods that raise food and fibre production.
Soil variables of special interest include texture, aeration and porosity, drainage, water content and water potential, horizonation, fertility, soil biota, and pH with cation-exchange capacity.
Its research covers irrigation and drainage, tillage, soil classification, plant nutrition and soil fertility, and newer areas such as greenhouse effect mitigation.
Erosion, compaction, lowered fertility and contamination remain serious concerns, and the field puts growing emphasis on keeping soils productive in the long term.
Pushing for maximum yield can carry high costs, such as massive crop diseases in monocultures or groundwater contamination from fertilizers and pesticides.
Soil husbandry is a strong tradition within the field.

title: Agroecology

definition.text: An academic discipline that studies ecological processes as they apply to agricultural production systems.

facts.text: The term can mean a science, a movement or a farming practice, and it is not tied to any single method such as organic, regenerative, integrated or industrial farming.
It is multidisciplinary, using sciences to study soil properties and plant-insect interactions and social sciences to study farming's effects on rural communities.
Ecosystem agroecology treats farms as integrated ecological systems, analysing their energy flows, nutrient cycles and the interactions between living and non-living components.
As a set of practices it harnesses ecological processes, biodiversity, nutrient recycling, agroforestry, intercropping and composting.
Biodynamic farming, organic agriculture and China's Green Food are the three certified forms; organics is the most widely practised, in 188 countries.
Wezel et al. date the first use of the term to 1928, by Basil Bensin; Tischler's 1965 book Agrarökologie may be the first titled 'agroecology'.
Researchers in agronomy, environmental science and related fields debate heatedly which model of agriculture or agroecology policy should support; the UN is perhaps its most prominent backer.

contested_note: Researchers disagree over which model of agriculture or agroecology public policy should support.

conflicts.text: Dalgaard et al. credit the German zoologist Friederichs with first using the name, in 1930.
conflicts.note: Wezel et al. instead give 1928 and Basil Bensin for the first use of the term.

title: Agroecosystem

definition.text: An ecological system that people manage and shape in order to farm.

facts.text: System properties studied in agroecosystems include productivity, stability, sustainability and equitability.
Harper's 1974 concept of agroecosystems, perhaps inspired by Tansley's process ecology of the 1930s, is considered the foundation of modern agroecology.
Erosion can irreparably reduce an agroecosystem's productive capacity, and cover crops are often grown for that reason alone.

notes: No page of its own; passes the 2+ in-scope pages test (Agroecology, Cover crop, Regenerative agriculture, Arbuscular mycorrhiza, Human impact on the nitrogen cycle).

definition.text: Growing a series of different crops on the same land over successive growing seasons.

facts.text: Rotation lessens a crop's reliance on one set of nutrients, cuts pest and weed pressure, and lowers the chance of resistant pests and weeds developing.
A well-designed rotation can reduce the need for synthetic fertilizers and herbicides and improve soil structure and organic matter, which reduces erosion.
Legumes such as alfalfa and clover hold nitrogen in root nodules; after harvest their leftover roots decay and release it to the following nitrogen-demanding crop.
Changing crops breaks pest life cycles and habitats; because plants of one family share pests and pathogens, rotations pay attention to plant family.
Rotations greatly increase soil organic carbon; long, highly diverse rotations do so most, while tillage disturbance drives an exponential decline.
In Brazil, conversion to no-till with intensive crop rotations sequestered soil organic carbon at 0.41 tonnes per hectare per year.

European farmers moved from two-field to three-field rotations between the 9th and 11th centuries; the later four-field sequence of wheat, turnips, barley and clover was key to the British Agricultural Revolution.
A faulty rotation can unbalance soil nutrients or build up pathogens, and the damage may take years to show and as long to correct.

definition.text: Agronomists' name for the yield benefit that crops gain from being grown in rotation.

facts.text: It comes broadly from relieving the drawbacks of monoculture; better nutrition, less pest, pathogen and weed stress, and better soil structure have been linked to it in some cases.
More soil organic matter under rotation improves water infiltration and retention, which raises drought tolerance and reduces erosion.
Less intensive tillage lets soil microbes thrive, and soil with low microbial activity supplies far fewer nutrients even when the same biomass is left in it.
Over time rotated crops can meet production goals with fewer purchased inputs.

definition.text: The use of crop sequences, residue and fallow management within a rotation to cut soil lost to erosion, often alongside zero or reduced tillage.

facts.text: Protection is greatest when the rotation leaves the most crop stubble on the surface, which slows overland flow and its power to detach and carry sediment.
Decomposing forage crops form binding products that glue particles into aggregates, which resist raindrop impact, water erosion and wind abrasion.
Where rain and drought are unpredictable, opportunity cropping, sowing only when soil water is adequate, gives better soil cover than a rigid rotation.
A field can be most vulnerable while fallow; in a decade-long study, fall rye sown after potato harvest cut soil run-off by as much as 43%.

definition.text: Choosing the crops of a rotation by what each adds to or takes from the field: organic matter, nutrients, pest control and protection from erosion.

facts.text: Crops are grouped by family, by nutrient needs and benefits, or by profitability, as cash crops versus cover crops.
Row crops such as vegetables are often the most profitable but tax the soil: low biomass and shallow roots leave little residue, and exposed soil loses organic matter faster.
Grasses and cereals, with dense, far-reaching roots, build soil structure and organic matter and compete with weeds for space and nutrients.
A nitrogen-fixing legume should precede a nitrogen-depleting crop, and a low-residue crop should be offset by a high-biomass cover crop.

definition.text: Farming that combines growing crops with keeping livestock, which helps manage rotations and cycle nutrients.

facts.text: Crop residues feed the animals and their manure replenishes crop nutrients, so nutrients cycle within the farm and less synthetic fertilizer is needed.
Livestock make efficient use of sod and cover crops, spreading their nutrients through the soil as manure instead of exporting them as sold hay.
Regenerative grazing of ruminants in mixed crop and grazing systems has improved soil nutrient cycling by speeding the decomposition of crop residues.

definition.text: Growing two or more crops in the same place at the same time.

facts.text: Intercropping and companion planting add diversity within one season; the Three Sisters plant corn with pole beans and squash, the beans supplying nitrogen and the squash a weed-suppressing canopy.
Double-cropping grows two crops in sequence in one season, or a crop alongside a cover crop, which suits small farms that cannot rest land under cover crops for long.
Rotations can be applied to both monocultures and polycultures, giving several ways to raise farm biodiversity in space and time.

definition.text: A farm management strategy that gathers and analyses data on time, place and individual plants or animals to fit decisions to variation across fields, for better efficiency, yield and sustainability.

facts.text: GPS lets farmers map the spatial variability of yield, topography, organic matter, moisture, nitrogen, pH, electrical conductivity and other soil variables.
It studies how terrain and soil properties affect crop growth and water distribution, aiming at a decision-support system for the whole farm.

Its first wave brought satellite and aerial imagery, weather prediction, variable rate fertilizer application and crop health indicators; the second added precise planting, topographic mapping and soil data.
Applying the right amount of inputs at the right place and time can cut nutrient and other input use while raising yields, which benefits soils and groundwater.
Its aims include matching inputs to crop needs and limiting nitrogen leaching; following GPS guidance lines also reduces soil compaction.
The concept emerged in the United States in the early 1980s; in 1985 University of Minnesota researchers varied lime inputs, and grid sampling at one sample per hectare appeared.
Soil moisture sensors and machine learning can time watering and deliver set amounts of fertilizer or water to the soil.

definition.text: Applying a material such as fertilizer at a rate that changes with the location or qualities of each part of a field, instead of uniformly.

facts.text: It is either map based, following prescription maps an advisor prepares in advance, or sensor based, calculated in real time by sensors on the applicator.
Prescription maps can be made with electromagnetic induction, which is considered cost-effective and non-destructive.
Nutrient needs differ across a field with soil properties and sunlight, so GPS-guided spreaders raise or lower the fertilizer rate as they go.
Variable rates of nutrients or pesticides can cut their use, saving costs and reducing harmful runoff into waterways.

definition.text: Differences in growing conditions within and between fields, which precision agriculture measures and manages.

facts.text: It arises from climate (hail, drought, rain), soils (texture, depth, nitrogen levels), cropping practices such as no-till, weeds and disease.
Permanent indicators, chiefly soil properties, describe a field's main constants, while point indicators track crop status such as disease, water stress or nitrogen stress.

Using soil maps, farmers adjust inputs predictively from static indicators such as soil, resistivity and field history, or by a control approach that updates them through the season by sampling and remote sensing.
Weather stations and sensors measuring soil electrical resistivity, along with satellite imagery, supply much of this information.

title: Irrigation

definition.text: Applying controlled amounts of water to land to help grow crops, landscape plants and lawns.

facts.text: Irrigation has been practised for over 5,000 years by many cultures; some of the earliest known use dates to the 6th millennium BCE in Khuzistan, south-west Iran.
Besides growing crops, it revegetates disturbed soils in dry areas, protects crops from frost, suppresses weeds in grain fields and prevents soil consolidation.
Water comes from groundwater, from rivers, lakes or reservoirs, or from treated wastewater, desalinated water, drainage water or fog collection.
It may supplement rainfall, as is common, or supply nearly all of a crop's water, which happens only in arid lands or outside the rainy season in semi-arid areas.
The main methods are surface (gravity) irrigation, the oldest; sprinkler irrigation; micro-irrigation such as drip; and subirrigation, which raises the water table.
Land equipped for irrigation reached 355 million ha in 2023, more than twice the 1960s area; 23% of croplands are equipped, and irrigated yields average 76% above rainfed ones.
Drainage is often studied with irrigation, and both are often needed together to sustain high crop production.
Over-irrigation raises water tables and causes irrigation salinity needing subsurface drainage, while under-irrigation gives poor salinity control and toxic salts build up at the surface.

notes: Extent figures differ by year within the page (352 million ha by 2021, 355 million ha in 2023; US 27 vs 25 million ha); kept only the 2023 set.

definition.text: The share of water applied to a field that the crop actually uses: field water efficiency is the water transpired by the crop divided by the water applied, times 100.

facts.text: Low efficiency means more water is applied than the crop or field needs, and the excess seeps or runs off, carrying nutrients or pesticides away.
Higher efficiency raises crop output per unit of water and cuts the water and pumping-energy cost of each unit of production.
It is improved by better system design, such as converting furrow to drip irrigation, or by better scheduling of when and how much to irrigate.
Sprinkler, drip or well-managed surface irrigation can reach 70% or more, but losses in practice are commonly 40% to 60%.

title: Drip irrigation

definition.text: A micro-irrigation method that lets water drip slowly to plant roots, from above or below the soil surface, placing it in the root zone to minimize evaporation.

facts.text: Properly managed, it can be the most water-efficient method, minimizing evaporation and runoff, with field water efficiency typically 80 to 90%.
Water runs through valves, pipes, tubing and emitters, and most large systems filter it so small particles do not clog the emitters.
Liquid fertilizer is often mixed into the water, called fertigation, with fertilizer savings of up to 95% reported; drip is also often combined with plastic mulch.
Buried clay pots were described in China in the first century BCE; the modern system was invented in Israel, and in 2023 3% of the world's farmers used drip.
Subsurface drip irrigation buries the drip line at or below the roots and is spreading where water is scarce or recycled water is used.
Localized watering cuts fertilizer loss by leaching, keeps the root zone at field capacity, lessens erosion and weeds, and keeps foliage dry against disease.
High-efficiency systems leach little, so salts from the water build up at the edge of the wetted zone; regular slight over-watering flushes them below the roots.
Running a system too long or too fast causes deep percolation below the root zone, so on sandy soils water is applied as slowly as possible.

notes: Re-anchored from Irrigation#Drip irrigation to the Drip irrigation article in the gap-fill pass.

definition.text: Irrigation in which water is piped to points in the field and sprayed overhead by high-pressure sprinklers or guns.

facts.text: Centre pivot systems carry sprinklers on wheeled towers that circle around a central water feed, and can irrigate all types of terrain.
Newer pivots hang drop heads just above the crop, or drag hoses that wet the ground directly, to limit evaporation; this is Low Energy Precision Application (LEPA).
Salty sprinkler water can burn leaves even where the soil is not saline.
Using sprinkler and micro-irrigation lowers the risk of waterlogging and erosion.

definition.text: Irrigation by artificially raising the water table so that the soil is moistened from below the plants' root zone.

facts.text: Long used for field crops where water tables are high, often on lowland or river-valley grassland, it uses pumps, canals, weirs and gates to set ditch water levels.
In greenhouses a nutrient solution floods potted plants from below for 10–20 minutes and is pumped back for reuse, saving water and nutrients.
Self-watering containers and wicking beds draw water up from a reservoir by capillary action.

definition.text: Watering crops with recycled or untreated municipal wastewater, whose nutrients can also fertilize them.

facts.text: Its nitrogen and phosphorus act as fertilizer, and the supply is cheaper than some sources and steady whatever the season or water restrictions.
Untreated wastewater is increasingly used in developing countries, often unsafely, with health hazards from pathogens and chemicals.
Risks include bacteria, heavy metals and organic pollutants such as pharmaceuticals and pesticides; effects on soil and plants depend on the wastewater and the soil.
WHO's 2006 guidelines advise a multiple-barrier approach, such as stopping irrigation a few days before harvest so that pathogens die off.

definition.text: The loss of water-soluble plant nutrients from soil, carried away by rain and irrigation water.

facts.text: Soil structure, crop planting and the type and rate of fertilizer are weighed to avoid excessive nutrient loss.
The term also covers deliberately applying a small excess of salty irrigation water so salts do not build up, which usually needs drainage to remove the extra water.
It becomes an environmental concern when seeping water carries dissolved chemicals into groundwater; in farming the main sources are excess fertilizer, poorly stored manure and biocides.
Leaching of nitrate from acidic sources can increase losses of calcium and other soil nutrients, lowering an ecosystem's productivity.
Areas with high rainfall become acidic through leaching.
Biochar and catch crops are among the measures used to reduce nutrient leaching.

definition.text: The loss of nitrate from soil as drainage water carries the excess ions, which soils do not hold, down to groundwater, streams and the sea.

facts.text: Nitrate and ammonium fertilizers are placed in the root zone because plants absorb them easily, but soils do not retain the surplus nitrate.
How much leaches depends on soil type and structure (sandy soils hold little water, clays much), how much water the crop uses and how much nitrate is already present.
Human nitrogen sources exceed natural ones by 50%, and leached fertilizers and manures make up 75% of them.
Nitrate in drinking water is linked to methemoglobinemia, or blue baby syndrome, so regulators cap it at 45 to 50 mg per litre.
Catch crops take up the nitrogen left over from fertilizing the previous crop, keeping it from being leached.

definition.text: The loss of phosphorus from fields by downward movement through the soil, an important pathway on flat, sandy land or soils prone to preferential flow.

facts.text: Unlike nitrogen, phosphorus adsorbs to soil particles, especially iron and aluminium oxides and hydroxides such as gibbsite and ferrihydrite, so soils rich in them can store fertilizer phosphorus.
Soils given more phosphorus than crops need, often for decades, have their sorption sites filled by this 'legacy phosphorus', so newly added phosphorus leaches.
Prolonged water saturation lowers redox potential and dissolves ferric iron minerals, releasing their phosphorus, a concern when restoring wetlands once drained for farming.
Phosphorus drives eutrophication of surface waters, and its loss from fields has long been seen as a major threat to water quality.

definition.text: The highest salt level a crop can withstand without losing productivity, beyond which it is harmed.

facts.text: The salt level is usually taken as the soil salinity or the salinity of the irrigation water.
It matters most on irrigated land in arid and semi-arid regions, where salinization is extensive and concerns hundreds of millions of hectares; saline land worldwide totals 3,230,000 km2.

Salty sprinkler water burns leaves; on an Australian scale, sensitive crops such as almond, apricot and citrus are affected below 178 mg/L chloride, tolerant ones such as cotton, sorghum and sunflower only above 710 mg/L.
Key studies include USDA Agriculture Handbook No. 60 in 1954, Maas and Hoffman's extensive study over 20 years later, and an FAO worldwide survey in 2002.
Most data come from pots, drums or lysimeters under controlled conditions; field data are rarer, but statistical methods can find tolerance levels in them.
Much research now aims to breed crops with higher salt tolerance for salinity-stricken regions.

title: Soil salinity classes for crops

definition.text: Bernstein's grouping of soils by the electrical conductivity of a saturated soil-paste extract (ECe), matched to the crops each class can still grow well.

facts.text: Soil salinity is most often expressed as ECe in decisiemens per metre, formerly millimhos per centimetre.
Bernstein's classes: ECe 0–2 non-saline; 2–4 slightly saline, sensitive crops lose yield; 4–8 moderately saline; 8–16 saline, only tolerant crops yield normally; above 16, only very tolerant crops.
Soil salinity control uses different bounds: saline only above ECe 4, slightly saline from 4 to 8, moderately saline from 8 to 16, severely saline above 16.
Schleiff ranks crop tolerance in 2 dS/m steps, from very sensitive below 2 to very tolerant above 10, narrower than the 4 dS/m steps in Richards' 1954 USDA handbook.

notes: Bernstein (S:902ba0a8e8ac) and Soil salinity control (S:0dc65d43a72f) use different class bounds; stated as two schemes, not a conflict.

definition.text: The ability of a crop to withstand the high salinity of irrigation with seawater or a mix of fresh water and seawater.

facts.text: Demonstration farms show some crops can grow on seawater; Dutch trials found that certain varieties of potato, carrot, red onion, white cabbage and broccoli thrive under salt-water irrigation.
Salt Farm Texel tests crops on 56 plots of 160 m2 at seven salt levels, from EC 2 to 35 dS/m, made by mixing fresh water with seawater of about 50 dS/m.
Thresholds there varied widely even within one crop: potato ranged from 1.9 dS/m for the variety Met to 4.1 dS/m for Mignonne.

title: Potting soil

definition.text: A substrate, also called growing medium or potting mix, used to grow plants in containers.

facts.text: Despite its name it usually holds little or no real soil, because soil compacts and loses pore space with repeated watering and is too heavy for pots.
Ingredients include peat, vermiculite, coconut coir, bark chips, wood fibre, perlite, mineral wool, sand, rice hulls and calcined clays, usually a mix of organic and inorganic materials.
A typical mix combines moisture-retaining materials, materials for aeration and drainage, and fertilizer, in ratios chosen for the plant.
Good media hold moisture and nutrients, take in water quickly, drain the excess, leave pore space for root oxygen, decompose slowly, support the plant and have suitable pH and cation exchange.
Peat is usually limed to cut its acidity, typically 8.5 pounds of limestone per cubic yard (5.0 kg/m3); dolomitic limestone is preferred because it supplies both calcium and magnesium.
Untreated coir holds too much sodium and potassium for plants, so it is washed and buffered with calcium and magnesium.
Peat use is controversial: harvesting degrades peatlands, which accumulate as little as 1 mm a year and store up to 30% of soil carbon on 3% of the world's surface.
Commercial potting soil is usually sterilized against weeds and plant diseases; Legionnaires' disease outbreaks have been traced to potting mix in several countries.

contested_note: Using peat in potting mixes is controversial because harvesting it degrades peatland habitats and carbon stores.

title: Specialty potting mixes
article: Potting soil#Different mixes for different uses

definition.text: Growing media adapted to a plant's, or a growth stage's, needs for aeration, drainage, nutrition and pH.

facts.text: Light germination mixes suit small seeds and seed-starting mixes larger ones; after early growth most plants prefer a better-draining potting mix.
Cacti and succulents need sharp drainage from a much larger share of perlite or sand, while carnivorous plants prefer the nutrient-poor, acidic soils of bogs and fens.
Cuttings root better in soilless mixes such as perlite, vermiculite, sand and sphagnum moss than in water.

definition.text: The main test of a potting mix's chemistry, which analyses a water extract of the mix.

facts.text: A soil test can be run on a potting mix even though it is not made of soil; for indoor home plants the mix is treated as a greenhouse medium.
Reference levels by this method: soluble salts optimally 2.0–3.5 mS/cm (acceptable 0.75–5.0), nitrate-N 100–200 ppm and phosphorus 6–9 ppm.
Nutrients missing from the bulk ingredients come from fertilizer, slow-release synthetics in conventional mixes or compost in organic ones, at most 1 part compost to 1 part bulking material.

title: Soilless growing substrates

definition.text: Inert or organic materials such as perlite or gravel that mechanically support plant roots in hydroponics, where plants grow without soil.

facts.text: Rock wool, spun from molten basalt or slag, is the most widely used medium; it holds much water and air, but its naturally high pH needs conditioning first.
Expanded clay pellets, fired at 1,200 °C until they swell and turn porous, are inert, pH-neutral, light and do not compact.
Coconut coir swells three to four times when wet and holds water well, but must first be washed of salts, tannins and phenolics, using 300–600 litres of water per cubic metre.
Perlite holds more air and less water than vermiculite, which wicks water and nutrients; adding perlite lowers a medium's water retention.

notes: Hydroponics itself is drafted by nutrients-and-plant-nutrition (Plant nutrition#Hydroponics); this entry covers only the substrate section.

title: Soil steam sterilization

definition.text: A farming technique that fully or partly sterilizes soil with steam, in open fields or greenhouses.

facts.text: Steam kills weeds, bacteria, fungi and viruses by heating soil enough to inactivate enzymes and coagulate vital cell proteins.
In the field it is a partial disinfection, since heat-resistant spore-forming bacteria survive and revitalize the soil; laboratory autoclaving achieves true sterilization.
It is now considered the best way to disinfect sick soil, potting soil and compost, and an alternative to bromomethane, which the Montreal Protocol curtailed.
Steaming relieves soil fatigue, the decline of soil health and fertility under poor management, and frees nutrients locked in the soil.
In integrated steaming the sterilized soil is recolonized by injecting a compost-based activator carrying beneficial microbes such as Bacillus subtilis.
Modern soil steaming was developed in Germany in 1888 and first used commercially in the United States in 1893; today superheated steam at 180–200 °C is often used.
Since the 2020s it has been adapted to construction and technosol production, killing seeds and weeds of invasive species in soil.

notes: Mushroom 'steam recycling' (S:ecf4c07b37b1) is flagged CONTESTED in the dossier; left out as a side use.

title: Soil steaming methods
article: Soil steam sterilization#Types of Soil Steaming In Practice

definition.text: The ways of applying steam to soil, grouped as substrate, surface and deep soil steaming, chosen by soil structure, crop and area to treat.

facts.text: Sheet steaming treats 15 to 400 m2 at once, reaching 25–30 cm depth and 90 °C in 4–5 hours; insulating fleece can save up to 50% of the energy.
Vacuum depth steaming, which draws steam down through buried or surface pipes, penetrates best, reaching up to 80 cm with fixed drainage pipes; the negative pressure technique reaches 60 cm.
Sandwich steaming pushes steam into the soil from the surface and from depth at the same time.
Stack steaming treats compost and substrates piled up to 70 cm high, kept to 1.5 hours at most to avoid condensed water in the bottom layers.

definition.text: A non-chemical pest control method that traps the sun's heat in soil until many soil-borne plant pathogens are killed or badly weakened.

facts.text: Moist soil is mulched and covered with a tarp, usually clear polyethylene, killing or weakening fungi, bacteria, nematodes, insect and mite pests, and weeds.
Soil must reach 35–60 °C, which kills pathogens in the top 30 cm; temperatures fall with depth.
It does not sterilize: it kills up to 90% of pathogens, while heat-tolerant beneficial microbes such as Bacillus survive and recolonize, making the soil more resistant to disease.
It can create disease-suppressive soils; in one study eight days of solarization killed all Verticillium dahliae at 25 cm depth.
Unlike conventional plasticulture, which protects crops in the coldest months, solarization covers soil in the hottest months to reach lethal temperatures.
It is the third approach to soil disinfestation, after steaming and fumigation, which date from the end of the 19th century.
First described in detail by Katan in 1976, it was studied in at least 24 countries within ten years and applied in more than 60 within thirty.
Concerns include the fate of the plastic sheets, the weaker weed control of biodegradable covers, and reduced microbial richness.

definition.text: An alternative to soil fumigation that adds organic amendments or compost before solarizing, so that microbial activity shortens the treatment.

facts.text: It is closely related to biofumigation and soil solarization, which use solar heat against nematodes, bacteria, fungi and other pests.
Spanish research on strawberry production found it sustainable and cost-effective, and small farms in California use it.
It can double as organic waste management, and food-industry residues can make it more efficient.

definition.text: The study of agrominerals, the minerals that matter to farming, their origins and uses; more broadly, geology applied to farm soil productivity and health.

facts.text: It combines geology, soil science, agronomy and chemistry, aiming to raise farm output by using geological resources to improve the chemical and physical properties of soil.
Agrogeologists work on replenishing soil fertility where unsustainable farming has depleted agrominerals.

The first project with major funding, the Tanzania-Canada project of 1989, helped farmers in southern Tanzania find and test local raw materials; raw materials have been used as fertilizer since the 1800s.

Other raw materials include apatite for slow phosphate release in acid soils, carbonates for liming, malachite against copper deficiency, scoria as a water-saving mulch and zeolite to conserve nitrogen.

definition.text: Phosphorite, a phosphorus-bearing sedimentary rock used as a sustainable, low-cost source of phosphorus for crops.

facts.text: Much conventional fertilizer added to phosphorus-deficient soils turns into insoluble complexes, so it has to be reapplied constantly.
Its phosphorus must be processed before plants and soil can take it up; fungi can solubilize it by producing organic acids.
Industry grinds the rock and adds water and sulfuric acid, removing impurities as gypsum, then treats the acidic phosphorus liquid with ammonia vapour to make granules.
A study in Zimbabwe found that mining dust mixed with processed fertilizer raised plant growth, phosphorus levels and organic carbon.

definition.text: Minerals, sometimes called stone bread, that matter to farming and horticulture because they can supply essential plant nutrients.

facts.text: Natural or processed, they serve as alternative fertilizers or soil amendments; the term dates from the 19th century.
Their use began with small-scale soil modification: perlite to improve aeration, pumice to curb evaporation, and vermiculite and zeolite to store moisture.
Research now seeks alternatives to potash, a major source of potassium and one of the original agrominerals, whose finite supply drives prices up.
They may also help with climate change mitigation, water conservation and soil management.

title: Soil remineralization

definition.text: Replenishing a soil's mineral nutrients by working crushed rock powder into it.

facts.text: Multi-nutrient rock fertilizers release potassium, calcium, magnesium and some phosphorus slowly, mimicking the natural weathering of parent material.
Rock powder can supply up to 5 years of nutrients: plants take what they need and the rest stays crystallized, whereas unabsorbed soluble fertilizer salts run off to groundwater.
Combined with organic fertilizer it has matched chemical fertilizer at much lower cost; it also raises soil pH and can use local mining waste.
It needs heavy application rates and releases nutrients slowly, so it cannot replace industrial fertilizers.
Dissolution depends on organic matter, pH and secondary clay precipitation, and lab rates can be 2–5 orders of magnitude higher than field rates.
Some volcanic and phosphate rocks contain toxic, heavy or radioactive elements.
Cations released from some powders react with carbon dioxide to form carbonate minerals, a potential carbon sink that could help mitigate global warming.

notes: Also draws on Agrogeology#Multi-nutrient rock fertilizers, which describes the same practice.

title: Land reclamation

definition.text: Creating new land from oceans, seas, riverbeds or lake beds; the result is called reclaimed land or land fill.

facts.text: Methods include infilling with heavy rock or cement topped with clay and dirt, draining submerged wetlands for farming, and dredging.
Egypt's Twelfth Dynasty (c. 2000–1800 BC) created farmland around Lake Moeris by diverting its water with levees and canals.
About 7,000 km2, almost a sixth of the Netherlands, has been reclaimed from sea, lakes, marshes and swamps; China has reclaimed more than 13,500 km2.
Reclaimed land is highly susceptible to soil liquefaction in earthquakes, and consolidation of soft ground is a common technical risk.
Fill compaction and drainage of wetlands enclosed by levees into polders both cause subsidence; drained marshes eventually sink below the surrounding water.
Draining wetlands for ploughing destroys habitat; nearly 65% of the Yellow Sea's tidal flats have been reclaimed, and some countries now restrict new projects.

notes: Different from Soil reclamation (Soil#Reclamation, drafted by what-soil-is), which restores degraded soil.

definition.text: Reclaiming land from the sea or from wetlands to make farmland, the main driver of reclamation before industrialisation.

facts.text: In South China farmers walled off shore areas near river mouths to make paddy fields, growing more salt-tolerant rice, or fish ponds.
Draining swampy or seasonally flooded wetlands turns them into productive farmland and also controls mosquitoes.
Salt marshes, once seen as coastal wastelands, were widely lost to reclamation for agriculture, urban development and salt production.

title: Regenerative agriculture

definition.text: A conservation and rehabilitation approach to farming that aims to regenerate topsoil, raise biodiversity and strengthen the health of farm soil.

facts.text: It is not one practice but a mix of sustainable techniques, such as minimal or no tillage, cover crops, crop rotations, compost and grazing.
A 2020 review of 229 articles found no legal or widely accepted definition: some definitions stress practices, others outcomes such as soil health and carbon sequestration.
Wageningen researchers found its four most consistent principles to be improving soil health, optimizing resource management, alleviating climate change and improving water quality and availability.
The Rodale Institute began using the term in the early 1980s.

A 2023 review found that reduced tillage, residue retention, cover cropping, crop-livestock integration and agroforestry can improve soil carbon, soil health or yields under some climates and soils, but results vary between agroecosystems.
An estimated 30–75% of global soil organic matter has been lost since tillage-based farming began.
Rotations that keep the ground permanently covered can raise soil fertility if they include nitrogen-fixing crops.
Its claims to mitigate climate change by sequestering carbon have been criticized by scientists as exaggerated and unsupported by evidence.

contested_note: Scientists dispute proponents' claims about how much carbon regenerative practices, especially holistic grazing, can sequester.

title: Holistic planned grazing

definition.text: Grazing that keeps rotating livestock herds between fields to mimic how natural herds graze.

facts.text: Trampling by herds is reported to aid soil restoration, plant regrowth, soil carbon storage and water infiltration.
Evidence on carbon gains is mixed: a meta-analysis of studies from 1972 to 2016 found Holistic Planned Grazing no better than continuous grazing for plant cover and biomass.
Adaptive multi-paddock grazing has reduced soil degradation compared with continuous grazing and, with rotations and permanent cover, may give net carbon sequestration.
A 2016 Swedish study put the realistic sequestration rate seven times lower than Allan Savory's claims and concluded that holistic management cannot reverse climate change.

contested_note: Studies disagree on whether holistic or adaptive grazing stores more soil carbon than continuous grazing.

title: Fallow

definition.text: Leaving arable land unsown for one or more growing cycles.

facts.text: Fallowing lets land recover and store organic matter while keeping moisture, and breaks pest and soil-borne pathogen cycles by removing their hosts.
Crop rotations traditionally left some fields fallow each year; under a two-field rotation, half the land lay fallow.
Intensive farming, including cover crops sown instead of fallow, has shrunk the area of fallow land, field margins and hedges.
A field can be most vulnerable to erosion while fallow, so keeping stubble cover, for example by zero tillage, is key to reducing soil loss.
Cover crops raised microbial biomass carbon by about 20% and particulate organic carbon by nearly 50% compared with bare or fallow ground.
In an improved fallow the rest period is enhanced, for example with a cover crop; with yellow sweetclover, weeds made up only 1–12% of standing biomass.
Clay soils hold nutrients better through their higher cation-exchange capacity, so more of their land can stay in production instead of lying fallow.

notes: Lead claim that fallows were the main habitat of farmland birds (S:2025650a13d6) carries a FAILED VERIFICATION tag; left out.

definition.text: Poor nutrient uptake by a crop after a fallow period because the soil lacks arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi.

facts.text: Susceptible crops such as corn should follow a cover crop that hosts the fungi, such as oats or another small grain, rather than a fallow.
Any plant roots, even those of weeds, reduce its occurrence.
Fields are now routinely cover-cropped to prevent erosion, suppress weeds, supply green manure and lower the risk of fallow syndrome.

definition.text: A substance, commonly called a weed killer, used to control unwanted plants.

facts.text: Selective herbicides control particular weeds and leave the crop largely unharmed; non-selective ones kill plants indiscriminately.
Together with nitrogen fertilizer and better cultivars, herbicides raised yields of major crops three to six times per acre between 1900 and 2000.
Before herbicides, weeds were controlled culturally, for example by changing soil pH, salinity or fertility.
Major breakthroughs came during the Second World War; glyphosate, marketed as Roundup from 1971, is now used very widely on resistant crops.
Herbicide use generally harms the environment, seriously damaging insects, non-target plants, animals and aquatic systems.
Weeds can evolve resistance; using herbicides with different modes of action slows selection for resistant types.
Well-designed crop rotations can reduce herbicide needs, while no-till practices may increase herbicide use.

definition.text: Herbicides applied to the soil before planting or crop emergence, taken up by the roots or shoots of emerging seedlings.

facts.text: Adsorption to soil colloids or organic matter often reduces the amount available for weeds to absorb.
They must sit in the right soil layer, placed mechanically or by rainfall; on the surface, volatilization and photolysis reduce their availability.
Many are absorbed by shoots still underground; EPTC and trifluralin are soil-applied, whereas glyphosate, 2,4-D and dicamba are applied to foliage.

definition.text: How long a herbicide stays active in soil: low residual activity if rain or soil reactions neutralize it within weeks or months, high if it stays potent for the long term.

facts.text: Some compounds can leave the ground almost permanently barren.
Atrazine, of the triazine family most feared for groundwater contamination, breaks down slowly in soils above neutral pH and can be carried by soil water to the water table, a 'carryover' effect.
Many modern herbicides are formulated to degrade within a short period after application.
How long herbicides persist depends on each compound's chemistry.

definition.text: Irrigation in which water is spread over the soil surface by gravity.

facts.text: It is by far the most common form of irrigation worldwide and has been practised in many places virtually unchanged for thousands of years.
Often called flood irrigation, implying uncontrolled and inefficient distribution, some forms such as surge irrigation are in fact closely managed.
An irrigation runs in four phases, advance, storage, depletion and recession; the depth applied at any point depends on the opportunity time water stands on the surface.
Border strip irrigation, a hybrid of basin and furrow methods, runs water down long, narrow bays between earth banks, often for dairy pasture.
Over-irrigation causes waterlogging and deep drainage, and rising water tables can lift salt from saline layers into the root zone.
Its relatively high leaching fraction makes salinization less of a problem than with other methods, but poor subsurface drainage can block salt leaching.
Long use of flood or surface irrigation leaves a recognisable irragric anthrosol.

definition.text: Surface irrigation through small parallel channels running down the field's main slope, with water flowing by gravity from the top end.

facts.text: Water speed depends on slope, roughness and furrow shape, but above all on the inflow rate and the soil's infiltration rate.
Furrows run from under 100 to 2,000 m long, depending on soil, site and crop, and suit row crops such as cotton, maize and sugar cane.
Slow advance soaks the top end more than the bottom; a faster advance improves uniformity and cuts the water needed.
Surge irrigation pulses the flow on and off; wetting and drying seal the surface and reduce infiltration, speeding advance, though quickly sealing clays gain little.

definition.text: Surface irrigation in which a level area enclosed by earth banks is flooded quickly and the water left to soak in.

facts.text: It is favoured on soils with relatively low infiltration rates, and traditional basins are not drained after irrigation.
Laser levelling and land grading allow large rectangular basins suited to mechanised broadacre cropping.
Drainback level basins pass water from each bay to a lower one in turn, a layout common in Australian rice and wheat rotations.

definition.text: Irrigation that diverts seasonal floods from normally dry river beds onto fields or into storage basins.

facts.text: It is an ancient method of arid and semi-arid lands in the Middle East, North Africa, West Asia, East Africa and parts of Latin America.
Floods lasting hours or days are diverted by intakes, spurs or bunds through channel networks to command areas from a few hectares to over 25,000 ha.
Fast floodwater moves large amounts of sediment, so river banks and beds can change rapidly.

title: Monocropping

definition.text: Growing a single crop year after year on the same land, also called continuous cropping.

facts.text: Maize, soybeans and wheat are often monocropped; farmers can grow only the most profitable crop with the same seed, pest control and machinery across the farm.
Repeating one crop gradually depletes certain soil nutrients and breeds pests and weeds adapted to that crop.
It damages soil ecology, reducing the diversity of soil nutrients and giving parasites an unbuffered niche, so the system leans more on pesticides and artificial fertilizers.
A single cultivar with one resistance strategy can be wiped out quickly by one opportunistic species, as in the Irish Great Famine of 1845–1849.
Monocropping is among the farming practices that aid soil erosion, while mixed cropping and crop rotation significantly reduce erosion rates.
Pesticides and fertilizers seeping into soil and groundwater from extensive monocropped acreage are a well-known concern.
Advocates say polyculture would be costly and unable to feed everyone; critics dispute this, citing monocropping's damage to societies and the environment.

contested_note: Advocates and critics disagree on whether monocropping's short-term food production outweighs its long-term costs to land, ecology and local economies.

definition.text: Pest control that combines non-chemical and chemical methods to keep pests in economic check while relying less on chemicals.

facts.text: The FAO describes it as integrating biological, chemical, physical and cultural strategies to grow healthy crops while minimizing pesticide use and its risks.
Prevention starts with cultural practices such as resistant varieties, crop rotation and intercropping.
It aims at control rather than eradication, accepting pest levels that are tolerable.
Pesticides are used only when needed, often timed to a stage of the pest's life cycle, which also helps protect water quality.

title: Land restoration

definition.text: Returning land to a different or earlier state for an intended purpose, which may include renaturalisation or rewilding.

facts.text: It counters human-caused degradation such as pollution, deforestation and salination, and differs from land reclamation, which alters or destroys ecosystems for cultivation or construction.
Projects choose a reference ecosystem to judge success and are managed adaptively, adjusting as the ecosystem responds.
Against desertification, soil is first fixed with grasses, shelterbelts and windbreaks to stop dunes moving, then enriched with nitrogen-fixing plants and crops grown in rotation.

notes: Adaptive management sentence (S:eba28ccea125) is flagged CONTESTED only for the word 'uncertain'; not a debate.

definition.text: Pest control in which a fumigant gas comes from fresh plant material chopped and buried in the soil to decompose.

facts.text: Brassicas such as mustard, cauliflower and broccoli release isothiocyanates from their glucosinolates, toxic to soil bacteria, fungi and nematodes but less persistent than synthetic fumigants; sorghum releases hydrogen cyanide instead.
Plants are chopped at flowering and worked into soil irrigated to field capacity, then covered with film for three or four weeks before planting.
It can also replenish soil nutrients and encourage beneficial organisms.
It is slow to take effect, can be costly if plants must be brought in, and is hard to standardize because cultivars differ in active content.

definition.text: A farming technique of digging pits in poorly permeable soil to catch water and concentrate compost.

facts.text: Pits are 15 to 50 cm across and 5 to 15 cm deep, spaced about 80 cm apart.
It is traditionally used in the western Sahel to restore degraded drylands and raise soil fertility, and has spread to semi-arid East Africa.
Filling the pits with manure and compost, reintroduced from the 1980s, attracts termites whose tunnels break up the soil; yields of trees, sorghum and millet can rise by up to 500 percent.

definition.text: The amount of a crop, or of a product such as milk or wool, produced per unit area of land.

facts.text: It is usually measured in kilograms per hectare or bushels per acre.
UK cereal yields rose from about 500 kg/ha in medieval times to 2000 kg/ha in the Industrial Revolution and 8000 kg/ha in the Green Revolution.
Fertilizer, better tools and farming methods, and improved crop varieties have raised yields.
In 2025 about 1.7 billion people lived in areas with sizeable degradation-induced yield losses; in rich countries intensive inputs sustain yields but mask the degradation.

definition.text: Sprinkler irrigation from equipment that rotates around a central pivot, watering a circular area of crop.

facts.text: A line of pipe segments carrying sprinklers rides on wheeled towers fed from the pivot; the standard 400-meter machine covers about 50 hectares.
Drops hang the sprinklers a few feet above the crop to limit evaporation and wind drift; LEPA systems release water directly onto the ground.
It needs less tillage than ground irrigation, reducing runoff, soil erosion and compaction.
Decades of pumping have emptied parts of the Ogallala Aquifer, with the water table dropping more than 1.5 m per year in places.

definition.text: An irrigation strategy that waters a crop during its drought-sensitive growth stages and limits water at other times.

facts.text: It accepts some drought stress and yield loss to reach the highest crop water productivity and stable yields rather than the highest yields.
Crop water productivity is marketable product per cubic meter of water; for cereals at field level it ranges from 0.10 to 4 kg/m3.
Cotton irrigation in Turkey and India could be cut to up to 60 percent of the crop's water requirement with limited yield loss, but maize, sensitive all season, suffers.
It reduces nutrient leaching from the root zone, but because water is used more efficiently the risk of soil salinization is higher than under full irrigation.

definition.text: Growing two or more crops at the same time in the same field, a form of polyculture.

facts.text: Its usual goal is a greater yield from a piece of land by using resources or ecological processes a single crop would leave unused.
In mixed intercropping crops are freely mixed; temporal intercropping pairs a fast-growing with a slow-growing crop; relay cropping sows the second crop while the first is growing.
Crop rotation is not intercropping, because its crops grow in separate seasons.
Crops are chosen not to compete for space, nutrients, water or light, for example a deep-rooted crop with a shallow-rooted one.
A legume intercrop has been found to increase soil diversity, and associated organisms may supply nutrients through nitrogen fixation.
In low-input or subsistence systems it can give higher yields for the same input, or more stable yields with less input.
Pest control by trap crops or push-pull cropping has had mixed success: of 100 trap-cropping examples reviewed in 2006, only 10 succeeded commercially.

definition.text: Growing strips of crops between rows of closely spaced trees or hedges.

facts.text: The trees are pruned before the crop is planted, and the cut leaves are spread over the crop area to supply nutrients; the hedges also act as windbreaks and reduce erosion.
Leguminous Inga trees fix nitrogen, grow on acid tropical soils, and drop a thick mulch that protects soil and roots and shades out weeds.
Inga alley cropping lets land be cultivated repeatedly, offering an alternative to slash-and-burn farming.
In the temperate strip-cropping variant, trees grow in wide strips rather than the single rows of alley cropping.

definition.text: A farming system that relies on natural, non-synthetic inputs such as compost, manure and green manure, with techniques such as crop rotation and mixed cropping.

facts.text: It aims at sustainability, soil fertility and biodiversity and, with rare exceptions, prohibits synthetic pesticides, synthetic fertilizers and genetically modified organisms.
It arose in the early 20th century partly because chemical farming brought soil compaction, erosion and declining fertility.
Albert Howard, called the father of organic farming, adopted Northbourne's term in An Agricultural Testament in 1940.
By 2022 about 96 million hectares in 188 countries were farmed organically by 4.5 million farmers, about 2 percent of world farmland.
A 2012 meta-analysis put organic productivity on average 25% below conventional, and a 2011 analysis found organic yields averaged 80% of conventional.
Nitrogen leaching and nitrous oxide emissions are lower per area but higher per amount of food, because organic yields are lower.
Lower yields can push more land into farming, which may cause biodiversity loss and negative climate effects.

definition.text: In organic farming, replacing the nutrients crops remove through the natural breakdown of organic matter, using green manure and composting.

facts.text: Soil organisms such as mycorrhiza and earthworms release the nutrients to plants through the growing season.
Supplying nitrogen when crops need it most is a challenge; legumes in rotations and green manures fix nitrogen with rhizobia.
Organic farmers also use animal manure, seed meal and mineral powders such as rock phosphate and greensand.
Farms without livestock find fertility harder to keep up and rely more on imported manure, which is bulky and costly to haul far.

title: Organic farming and soil quality

definition.text: The dispute over whether organically managed soils end up better or worse than conventionally farmed ones.

facts.text: Supporters say organically managed soil has higher quality and water retention, which may raise yields in drought years.
Organic farming can build soil organic matter better than conventional no-till; a 2007 USDA study found manure in tilled organic systems built soil better than no-till.
An 18-year study on nutrient-depleted soils in cold-temperate climates found conventional methods better for fertility and yield, crediting organic gains to imported materials.
Gunsmoke Farms, a 137 square kilometre organic project in South Dakota, suffered massive erosion from tillage after converting.

contested_note: Studies disagree on whether organic methods build soil fertility better than conventional or no-till farming.

definition.text: A period in which technology transfer initiatives produced a large increase in crop yields.

facts.text: Its approach combined high-yielding cereal varieties, expanded irrigation, modern management, hybrid seeds, synthetic fertilizers and pesticides.
High-yielding varieties take up more nitrogen, carry semi-dwarfing genes against lodging, and outperform traditional varieties only with enough irrigation, pesticides and fertilizer.
Norman Borlaug, called the father of the Green Revolution, received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970.
By a 2021 estimate it raised yields by 44% between 1965 and 2010; cereal production in developing nations more than doubled from 1961 to 1985.
Energy inputs rose faster than output, and its machinery and agrochemicals tie farming to crude oil.
Over-farming has caused soil contamination, erosion and degradation, and soil nutrient depletion pushed farmers to clear forest.
Nitrogen fertilizer applied beyond crop needs, such as broadcast urea, emits nitrous oxide and pollutes water.
Wheat bred to tolerate acid, aluminium-rich soils opened the Cerrado savanna to farming.

definition.text: Coconut husk fibre, whose processed form, coco peat, is used in potting mixes and as a substitute for peat.

facts.text: Concern over the sustainability of extracting peat has increased use of coir as an alternative substrate.
Coco peat holds water like a sponge: 1 kg of dry coco peat expands to 15 litres moist, with a pH of 5.5 to 6.5.
It is high in sodium and potassium, so it is buffered with a calcium solution; its potassium can cause magnesium and calcium deficiencies.
It is low in nutrients, and incompletely decomposed coco peat ties up nitrogen as it breaks down.

definition.text: An organobromine gas, CH3Br, long used as a fumigant and soil sterilant.

facts.text: It was widely applied as a soil sterilant, mainly for seed production but also for crops such as strawberries and almonds, and was safer and more effective than some other sterilants.
Because it releases ozone-destroying bromine radicals, the Montreal Protocol phased it out, with developed countries reaching 100% reduction by 2005.
Its loss pushed seed growers towards soil steam sterilization, mechanical roguing and fallow seasons.
Alternatives include chloropicrin, 1,3-dichloropropene and methyl isothiocyanate, which spreads through soil less well and needs much more irrigation to activate.

title: Dryland farming

definition.text: Growing crops without irrigation, typically in regions where a cool wet season charges the soil with the moisture crops will use in the following dry season.

facts.text: Dry farming depends on the bank of soil moisture built up by winter rain, and grain crops grow on that stored water rather than growing-season rainfall.
It is possible with as little as 230 millimetres of precipitation a year.
Practices include wide plant spacing, controlled traffic, minimal tillage and strict weed control so weeds do not use the stored moisture.
Summer fallow grows one crop on two seasons' precipitation, leaving stubble and residue to trap snow.
Old claims that tillage seals in moisture as a dust mulch did not stand up to testing: tillage actually increases evaporation losses.
It is especially prone to wind erosion, and fallow years leave fields without protective cover.

Some moisture-saving techniques, such as frequent tillage, conflict with saving topsoil, whose preservation is usually the most important long-term goal; windbreaks, no-till, mulch and strip farming help.

contested_note: One passage calls dust mulching controversial, while another says testing showed tillage increases evaporation.

definition.text: A lightweight, porous aggregate made by heating clay to about 1,200 °C in a rotary kiln, often called LECA.

facts.text: Heating expands gases trapped in the clay into thousands of small bubbles, and the pellets come in sizes from 0.1 to 25 millimetres and densities of 250 to 510 kg/m3.
Mixed into heavy soil it improves aeration and drainage; blended with soil and peat it adds compaction resistance and holds water during drought.
In hydroponics its round pellets aerate the roots while the clay soaks up water and nutrients for a steady supply.
In semi-hydroponics a pot of LECA stands in a nutrient reservoir and the porous pellets wick moisture up to the roots.

definition.text: Growing a single crop species in a field at one time.

facts.text: Monoculture and polyculture describe crop diversity in space, whereas monocropping and crop rotation describe diversity over time.
It eases planting and harvesting in the short term, but reduced biodiversity and nutrient depletion make it more vulnerable to pests and disease over time.
Perennial monocultures such as oil palm, sugarcane, tea and pines can acidify and degrade soil and encourage soil-borne diseases.
As soil health declines more synthetic fertilizer is used, and excess nitrogen can leach into ground and surface waters.

definition.text: Growing two or more crops on the same land within one year instead of just one.

facts.text: Crops grown at the same time count as intercropping, while double-cropping plants a second crop after the first is harvested.
In the Garhwal Himalaya, barahnaja sows 12 or more crops on one plot and harvests them at different times.
It can cut input costs and lower the risk of weeds, pests and disease through relationships between the crops.
Only 5% of global rainfed cropland is multiple cropped, against 40% of irrigated cropland.

definition.text: An ecological farming approach set out by Masanobu Fukuoka, also called the Fukuoka method or do-nothing farming.

facts.text: Fukuoka reduced it to five principles: no tillage, no fertilizer, no pesticides or herbicides, no weeding and no pruning.
The ground stays covered with weeds, clover and legumes that are cut and left to return nutrients, and the previous crop's straw mulches the topsoil.
It is meant as a closed system needing no human-supplied inputs, and after 25 years Fukuoka's farm gave yields comparable to Japan's most advanced farms.
Rather than build terraces, Fukuoka prevented soil erosion by growing trees and shrubs on slopes.

title: Shifting cultivation

definition.text: A farming system in which a plot is cropped for a while and then abandoned to fallow regrowth while the cultivator moves to another plot.

facts.text: Cropping usually stops when the soil shows signs of exhaustion or, more often, when weeds overrun the field.
The cropping period is usually shorter than the fallow period during which the land regenerates.
Land is often cleared by slash-and-burn, and the ashes add potash to the soil.
One of the first forms of agriculture, its survival suggests it is a flexible and highly adaptive way of producing food.
Population growth, cash crops and chainsaws have shortened fallows and lengthened cropping periods.
Permanent cultivation of fragile tropical soils after one slash-and-burn cycle, with little nutrient replacement, can degrade them rapidly.
The FAO named it a cause of deforestation while excluding logging, provoking a confrontation with environmental groups.

contested_note: The FAO blamed shifting cultivators for deforestation, a view environmental groups and later observers dispute.

definition.text: A form of shifting cultivation in which forest or woodland plants are cut and burned to create a field called a swidden.

facts.text: Burning the dried slash leaves a nutrient-rich ash layer that raises soil fertility and temporarily removes weeds and pests.
After about three to five years nutrient depletion and weeds cut yields, the plot is abandoned, and recovery takes from five to more than twenty years.
Roughly 200–300 million people use it.
Because leached tropical soils such as those of the Amazon are extremely poor, it is one of the few kinds of farming possible there.
It needs much land or few people; burned too often, as populations grow, the forest is eventually destroyed.
Charring rather than fully burning the slash and ploughing the charcoal in (slash-and-char) has been proposed to boost yields.

definition.text: Farming that reduces environmental harm, sustains and expands natural resources and uses non-renewable resources productively.

facts.text: The USDA defined it in 1977 as an integrated, site-specific system that over the long term meets food needs and enhances environmental quality and the resource base.
It aims to prevent harm to soil, water, biodiversity and downstream resources, and can include permaculture, agroforestry, mixed farming, multiple cropping and crop rotation.
Erosion from farm fields is estimated at 10 to 20 times the soil formation rate under no tillage and more than 100 times under conventional tillage.
Over a billion tonnes of southern Africa's soil erode each year, which if continued would halve crop yields within thirty to fifty years.
Intensive agriculture lowers soil carbon, harming structure and crop growth, while changed practices can turn soil into a carbon sink.
A sustainably managed wheat farm had more organic matter, microbes and nutrients than an adjacent conventional farm, and 22.4% higher net returns despite slightly lower yields.
Microplastics from plastic mulch, compost, sewage sludge and dirty irrigation water can alter soil structure and microbial communities.
Phosphate-solubilizing microorganisms and mycorrhizae release phosphorus fixed by aluminium, calcium and iron, making rock phosphate more effective.

title: Soil sickness

definition.text: A decline in soil fertility and crop yield, often after long-term monoculture, marked by a shift in harmful and beneficial soil microbes.

facts.text: In 1832 the Swiss botanist De Candolle suggested that exudates from crop plants caused soil sickness.
In aged tea plantations, polyphenols building up in the soil shift microbial communities and contribute to soil sickness.

notes: Syllabus phrase 'Replant disease'; no crawled sentence uses that term, so the entry follows the sources' term soil sickness.

definition.text: The injection of fertilizers and other water-soluble products into an irrigation system.

facts.text: It is used to add nutrients or correct deficiencies found by plant tissue analysis, mostly on high-value crops such as vegetables, turf, fruit trees and ornamentals.
Nitrogen, the most common nutrient supplied, comes as anhydrous ammonia, ammonium nitrate or urea; phosphorus comes as ammonium phosphates and potassium as muriate of potash.
Delivering nutrients with the water allows micro-dosing at a precise time and rate and reduces leaching.
Drip fertigation, especially subsurface drip, can raise fruit and flower yield and quality; most systems need a backflow preventer to protect drinking water.

definition.text: Mineral wool is a fibrous material spun or drawn from molten rock or slag, used among other things as a hydroponic growth medium.

facts.text: Mineral wool products can be engineered to hold large amounts of water and air for root growth and nutrient uptake, and the fibres give mechanical support.
Its naturally high pH makes it unsuitable at first, so it needs conditioning, for example pre-soaking in nutrient solution at pH 5.5 until it stops bubbling.
Stone wool is made by blowing air or steam through molten rock at about 1600 C, giving fine intertwined fibres 2 to 6 micrometres across.

definition.text: Different cover crop plants are grown for different primary purposes.

facts.text: Grasses such as cereal rye and oats catch and cycle nutrients; legumes such as hairy vetch and red clover fix nitrogen with Rhizobium as green manures.
Fast-growing competitive species such as buckwheat and sorghum-sudangrass smother weeds; brassicas such as mustards and radishes biofumigate pests with glucosinolates and isothiocyanates.
Strong-rooted crops such as cereal rye, radishes, hairy vetch and alfalfa loosen compacted soil; sorghum-sudangrass, cereal rye and sunn hemp build biomass and organic matter.
Ecologists separate canopy functions (aboveground biomass) from root functions (belowground biomass), and choice can follow the traits wanted.
Grass cover crops are more likely than legumes to increase soil organic matter; some grow as much or more biomass underground as above.
Hairy vetch or crimson clover may yield 1.5 to over 4 tons dry weight per acre; mature cereal rye 3-5 tons; early-terminated crops as little as half a ton.
A five-year California clover experiment raised organic matter in the top 2 inches from 1.3% to 2.6%.
Pooled experiments found cover crops raised organic matter 8.5% over original levels and soil nitrogen 12.8%.

definition.text: Leguminous plants are often very good cover crops, grouped as summer annuals, winter annuals, and biennial or perennial legumes.

facts.text: Summer annuals include soybeans, cowpeas and sunn hemp; winter annuals include winter field peas, crimson clover, hairy vetch, Balansa and subterranean clover; red clover, white clover and alfalfa are perennials, sweet yellow clover a biennial.
Crimson clover suits mild climates, matures quickly and gives a large nitrogen contribution, but is marginal in hardiness zone 5, colder zones, and on poorly drained or calcareous soils.
Austrian winter and Canadian field peas can leave 2.5 tons or more of dry matter and fix 100-150 or more pounds of nitrogen per acre.

Cowpeas are native to Central Africa, thrive in heat and drought and on low-fertility soils, but even mild frost kills them; berseem clover gives dense cover that suppresses weeds and is unlikely to cause livestock bloat.
Sweet clover is a hardy biennial whose roots penetrate compacted subsoil; it needs near-neutral pH and high calcium and does poorly in wet clayey soils.
Red clover is vigorous and shade tolerant, and is interseeded into small grains in early spring because it starts slowly and competes little.

definition.text: Grass cover crops include annual cereals (rye, wheat, triticale, barley, oats), forage grasses such as ryegrass, and warm-season grasses such as sorghum-sudangrass.

facts.text: Their fibrous root systems scavenge leftover nutrients, especially nitrogen, and some establish rapidly to greatly reduce erosion.
They produce large amounts of residue and roots that add organic matter, and the residue helps suppress weed germination.
Cereal rye grows in late fall and early spring as a catch crop and soil conditioner in cool regions, and is widely used in Maryland to cut nutrient loading into the Chesapeake Bay.

definition.text: Buckwheat is a frost-sensitive summer annual cover crop that completes its life cycle quickly.

facts.text: It takes about six weeks from planting in warm soil to early flowering, can exceed 2 feet in a month, and grows better than many cover crops on low-fertility soils but tolerates compaction poorly.
It competes well with weeds and has been reported to suppress root pathogens including Thielaviopsis and Rhizoctonia.
Its seeds do not persist for years but it can reseed as a volunteer weed, so mow, roll or till it before seeds develop.

article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Building_Soils_for_Better_Crops_-_Ecological_Management_for_Healthy_Soils_4e_(Magdoff_and_van_Es)/10%3A_Cover_Crops/10.03%3A_Types_of_Cover_Crops#Other Crops > Cover Crops In Perennial Systems
title: Cover crops in perennial systems

definition.text: In orchards and vineyards, groundcover or floor management with perennial cover crops can improve soil health and crop quality.

facts.text: The cover should not overly compete with the main crop and should persist with little maintenance while giving erosion and weed control, tolerating shade, traffic and drought.
It acts as a living mulch; Dutch white clover gives modest nitrogen, and low-growing fescues with dense fine roots need minimal mowing.
In vineyards covers are sometimes kept away from the vines but used to compete with them and curb excess vegetative growth.

definition.text: Mixtures of cover crop species offer combined benefits, the most common being a grass with a legume.

facts.text: Mixed stands usually suppress weeds better than a single species, and legumes with small grains offset the nitrogen decline when grains mature.
In the mid-Atlantic, a rye-hairy vetch mix manages nitrogen: rye is stimulated when much nitrate remains, reducing leaching, while vetch competes better and fixes more when little is available.
Erect rye supports vetch, and vetch held up by rye is killed more easily by close mowing, which may replace herbicide in no-till.

definition.text: Cover crops can supply nitrogen to the next crop or lower available nitrogen at season end to cut losses.

facts.text: A productive legume grown to bud stage can make 70 to well over 100 pounds of nitrogen per acre available; hairy vetch and crimson clover are frequent choices.
Supply depends on growth stage, biomass and nitrogen content; small deep-green plants contain over 3 percent N but little total N.
Cereal rye N falls below 1 percent with a C:N ratio of 80 or more at maturity; at about 1.5-2 percent N, soil organisms use all the nitrogen and little reaches the next crop.

definition.text: A cover crop can be planted for a whole growing season, after the cash crop harvest, or interseeded into a growing cash crop.

facts.text: A full-season high-biomass mix builds the most organic matter and suits infertile or eroded soils and organic transition, but no income crop grows that year.
Most farmers sow after harvest, avoiding competition with the main crop; seed can be no-till drilled for better stands, and tillage before seeding should be avoided.
The choice depends on the goal, cash crops, season length and climate.

title: Planting green

definition.text: Planting green is seeding a cash crop directly into a still-living cover crop and terminating the cover soon after.

facts.text: Older advice left a week or two between killing the cover and planting, which remains best in a dry spring.
The cover is usually sprayed shortly after planting, or suppressed mechanically with a rolling stalk chopper or a cereal-rye roller-crimper ahead of a no-till planter.
It has worked for soybeans, corn and cotton but is not recommended for most direct-seeded vegetables.

definition.text: Cover crops are killed or drastically weakened before or during soil preparation for the next cash crop.

facts.text: Methods include mowing after flowering, herbicide with no-till, plowing in, mow-roll-crimp with no-till planting in one pass, and winter injury.
Waiting a week or two lets residue decompose, easing nitrogen immobilization, allelopathy, damping-off, cutworm and wireworm problems, and a better seedbed.
A sudex cover crop is especially allelopathic, so tomatoes, broccoli and lettuce should wait six to eight weeks.

definition.text: Cover crops can cause serious problems if not managed carefully.

facts.text: They can deplete soil moisture, become weeds, compete with an intercropped cash crop for water, light and nutrients, and cost seed and establishment.
In dry areas and on sands, late killing of a winter cover may cause moisture deficiency; in warm humid no-till climates longer growth means less wet soil at planting and more residue.
Cover crops raise infiltration through macropores and water-holding capacity through organic matter, and residue slows runoff.
