title: Cover crops and plant-parasitic nematodes

definition.text: Cover crop choice can limit nematode damage, because species differ in host status.

facts.text: Grain crops are nonhosts of root-knot nematode (M. hapla), so growing grains reduces numbers; very bad infestations may need two full grain seasons.
Root-lesion nematode (P. penetrans) infects most crops; a legume such as hairy vetch will stimulate it, while sudangrass, sorghum-sudan, ryegrass and pearl millet reportedly cut numbers.
Suppression comes from poor host status, stimulated microbial antagonists and toxic products released on decomposition; brassicas and pearl millet also biofumigate.

definition.text: Cropping systems can be diversified over time, across the farm landscape, or with perennials, trees and livestock.

facts.text: Diversity over time comes from cover crops and rotations; spatial diversity from different crops in different fields or strips; a staggered rotation gives both.
Perennials add diversity with less frequent rotations, for example dairy farmers growing alfalfa three to four years before corn; agroforestry and integrated livestock add further dimensions.
An ecological principle behind this is that diversity contributes to stability and productivity.

definition.text: Crop type, yield, root mass, harvested portion and residue management together set soil organic matter under a rotation.

facts.text: Planting row crops on virgin forest or prairie soil drops organic matter rapidly for five to ten years until a low equilibrium is reached, which then holds if practices stay unchanged.
Switching to grass or grass-legume sod raises organic matter, but more slowly than the loss under continuous tillage.

In a 60-year Missouri experiment, continuous corn lost over 9 inches of topsoil (21 tons per acre a year) and ended with 1.2% organic matter, against 2.2% under unfertilized timothy; a six-year rotation kept about 70% of the timothy topsoil.
In eastern Canada, continuous corn added about 100 pounds of organic matter per acre yearly, corn-alfalfa 500, four-year alfalfa 800; 3% organic matter is about 60,000 pounds per acre.
Perennial forages slow decomposition by reducing disturbance and add organic matter from sod roots, part of which die each year; older grass roots die even during the growing season.
Organic matter gains plateau once mineral surfaces are saturated and the soil is highly aggregated, however much residue, manure or compost is added.
In semiarid Oregon, total microorganisms under a two-year wheat-fallow system were about 25% of the amount under pasture.
Moldboard plow tillage decreases earthworm and other soil organism populations; including perennial forages enhances the diversity effect.

definition.text: The active rooting period is the percent of a rotation during which living roots are present.

facts.text: It runs from 32% for corn-soybeans to 57% for soybean-wheat and 76% for a three-year soybean-wheat-corn rotation.
Adding winter wheat to a corn-soybean alternation greatly lengthens it, because winter annuals, perennials and cover crops extend the growing period beyond summer annuals.
Longer living cover decreases erosion, nitrate loss and groundwater contamination.
Dry beans-winter wheat with a cover crop reached 92% with three species.

definition.text: Diversified rotations offer benefits over very simple ones, including better water quality and lower nitrous oxide loss.

facts.text: In South Dakota, a four-year corn-field pea-winter wheat-soybean rotation beat corn-soybean with higher soybean yield, more soil organic matter and less nitrous oxide lost.

Spring-planted annuals leave soil without roots for much of the year, so nitrate can leach, a problem accentuated by tile drainage in the Midwest and Northeast; bare wetter soil also runs off and erodes more.
Perennial forages and winter grains protect water; cover crops help similarly but do not substitute for a good rotation, and the combination gives the greatest improvement.

definition.text: Diversified rotations spread labor and reduce exposure to price swings, but add equipment and management demands.

facts.text: Forage hay and early-harvested crops spread labor over the season, easing management by family labor and giving steadier income.
Costs include more equipment and labor conflicts, such as cultivating corn at the same time as harvesting hay.
Integrated livestock with multi-species grazing need less specialized equipment, harvest and spread manure themselves, and diversify income.

definition.text: Carefully chosen rotations, especially alternating grains and broadleaf plants, help control plant diseases and nematodes.

facts.text: Some diseases need only a one-year break; others need several years of nonhost crops to cut inoculum.
Pulse crops seem to stimulate beneficial organisms and reduce cereal root disease; a multiyear broadleaf break lowers common root rot of wheat and barley.
Rotation is hard for wide-host-range pathogens, seed-borne disease and windborne wheat leaf rust, which need other tactics.

definition.text: A set of guidelines for designing a new crop rotation.

facts.text: Follow a legume forage with a high-nitrogen crop such as corn, and grow oats, barley and wheat less in the second or third year after the sod.

Grow the same annual crop only one year and avoid closely related species in sequence, since pests and diseases are shared; western corn rootworm populations have lately emerged that survive corn-soybean alternation.
Plant nonhost grains for root-knot nematodes for a few years before a susceptible crop such as carrots or lettuce.
Small grains suppress weeds, row crops allow cultivation, and mowed or grazed sods control annual weeds; use longer perennial periods on sloping, erosive land.
Deep-rooted crops such as alfalfa, safflower or sunflower scavenge subsoil nutrients and water, and their root channels aid infiltration.

In limited-rainfall regions, water use is critical: hay and sunflowers may leave too little moisture; under 25% of rain during the 14-month fallow in the Central High Plains reaches the next wheat crop.

title: Historic rotations and the corn-soybean rotation

definition.text: Rotations should suit each farm's soil, climate, resources and economics, so only historic examples can guide.

facts.text: A five- to seven-year rotation on northern Midwest and Northeast mixed farms put nitrogen-hungry corn after pasture, grain only two of five to seven years, and oats as a nurse crop when hay was seeded; it roughly maintained organic matter.
Cheap pesticides and fertilizer, feedlots, export markets and price-support programs narrowed production to corn and soybeans.
The corn-soybean rotation beats monoculture but brings erosion, nitrate and herbicide pollution, organic matter loss and sometimes more insects; soybeans leave minimal residue.

definition.text: Silvopasture integrates trees and grazing livestock on the same land.

facts.text: It gives forest products and forage, so both short- and long-term income.
Partial shade helps cool-season grasses in heat in temperate climates, and keeps animals cool in hot ones.
It still needs agronomic care such as forage selection, fertilization and rotational grazing, and can stabilize landslide-prone slopes.

definition.text: Forest farming grows understory crops within an established natural or timber forest, without separate growing zones.

facts.text: Shade is desired; examples are ginseng, mushrooms, elderberries, rhododendrons and moss, many quite profitable.

definition.text: Faidherbia albida is a tropical legume tree of seasonally dry climates used in silvopasture and alley cropping.

facts.text: Its feathery leaves give a light canopy for corn or pasture, and it has a deep taproot.
It carries foliage in the dry season when forage is scarce, blooms for bees at the dry season's end, and gives pods for livestock and wood for fuel.

definition.text: Transitional systems exploit shading and microclimate change as trees mature.

facts.text: A landowner may start with alley cropping between young trees, then move to silvopasture, forest farming or an orchard, or trim the trees and keep alley cropping.
